### **Cycle 113 Newsroom Continuity Brief**

**Selected Sources:**
* *The Cycle Pulse — Y3C7* (Cycle 111) [1–63]
* *The Cycle Pulse — Y3C8* (Cycle 112) [64–118]

---

### **1. Housing Stabilization & Municipal Accounting (West Oakland)**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Legislative Baseline & Funding:** Proposed by **Mayor Avery Santana** and enacted in **Cycle 78** on a 6–3 Council vote (**Ramon Vega** yes, **Leonard Tran** no, **Elliott Crane** yes remotely), the **West Oakland Stabilization Fund** holds a total budget of **\$28,000,000** [1-3].
* **Disbursement Milestones:**
  * In **Cycle 111 (Y3C7)**, Month Ten cleared a **\$400,000** payment, bringing the total to **91 households stabilized** with **\$22,600,000** remaining [1, 4, 5].
  * In **Cycle 112 (Y3C8)**, Month Eleven cleared another **\$400,000** payment, maintaining the **23-day average processing window** [6-8].
  * Cumulative disbursements surpassed **\$5,000,000**, leaving **\$22,200,000** remaining in the fund balance [8].
* **City Treasury Balance:** The city treasury received **\$5,100,000** in Cycle 112 (\$5,000,000 from weekly allocations plus \$122,035 in court funds across 27 cleared charges), closing at **\$115,400,000** (up from \$110,300,000) [9, 10].
* **Behind-the-Scenes Administrative Pipeline:** OEWD Program Director **Marcus Webb** noted after work in Cycle 112 that **six household files remain stalled in the queue waiting on title search** [6, 11].
* **Neighboring Initiatives:** The **West Oakland Tenant Defense Fund** (\$4.2M budget) was scheduled for a vote in Cycle 112, while **Commercial Stabilization for Grand Lake** (\$2.5M budget) remains filed at the legislation stage [12].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 113**
* **Accounting & Processing Discrepancies:** Editor-in-Chief **Mags Corliss** and civic reporter **Carmen Delaine** infer that the 23-day mean processing standard masks severe delays for individual applicants, while public ledgers fail to provide household addresses or show where disbursed funds land after leaving the treasury [4, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13].
* **The Human Cost of Title Delays:** Marcus Webb's personal audit highlights that administrative spreadsheets count compliance without tracking whether any of the six title-delayed households face imminent displacement [6, 11, 13].
* **Entering Cycle 113:** The scheduled **Month Twelve disbursement review in Cycle 113** will test whether the six title-delayed files clear or lengthen, and whether case-level processing metrics are made public [8, 14, 15].

---

### **2. Athletics Offseason "Roster Math", Vinnie Keane's Future & Analytics**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **World Series Title & Parade Bus:** In Cycle 111 (Y3C7), the **Oakland Athletics** won Game 5 to secure their **seventh World Series championship under General Manager Mike Paulson**, led by pitcher **John Ellis** (6 IP, 2 ER, 5 K) and home runs from **Eric Taveras**, **Darrin Davis** (3-for-4), and **Mark Aitken** [16-18].
* **End-of-Era Reflections:** On the Downtown double-decker parade bus, **Mike Paulson**, **Vinnie Keane**, and **Benji Dillon** rode at the front [19, 20]. **Mark Aitken** (*"saying goodbye to something"*), **Benji Dillon** (*"finally okay to put it down"*), and **Mike Paulson** (*"doing the math in your head — who stays, who goes"*) openly reflected on impending retirement and roster shifts [5, 30–32].
* **The Blue Lattern Bar Farewell (Y3C8):**
  * Columnist **P Slayer** covered a farewell gathering for Vinnie Keane and Benji Dillon at the **Blue Lattern Bar** in Jack London [67, 97–100].
  * Fans **Jire Hilt** and **Lila Patty** bought new Athletics jerseys; Lila cleared her head near a local construction site [21, 22].
  * Vinnie Keane stated he was *"still getting used to not being as active with the A's"* and called the event a mix of nostalgia and celebration [23, 24]. Keane also appeared at an **Or Hashalom Renewal Community** health fair praising neighborhood support for the team [25, 26].
  * Benji Dillon noted underlying friction and tension among attendees who felt uneasy about the farewell [23, 27].
* **Keane 2041 Dossier Audit (Elliot Marbury Data Desk):**
  * In 2041, Vinnie Keane struck out **6 times in 127 at-bats** (1 per 21.2 ABs) with **13 home runs** (.701 SLG) and **0 walks** across 37 games [23, 28-30].
  * Marbury proved this strikeout rate is an **outlier on a thin 127 AB sample**, compared to his 16-season career baseline (where his best full-workload rate was 1 SO per 8.4 ABs in 2028 on 616 ABs) [67, 91–93, 96].
  * 2041 peer comparisons: **Martin Richards** (1 SO per 6.6 ABs over 463 ABs; career contact rate improved across 2039–2041) and **Darrin Davis** (1 SO per 8.9 ABs over 374 ABs) [6, 52–55, 94].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 113**
* **The Public Farewell Contradiction:** Mags Corliss and P Slayer infer a stark contradiction between hosting a public farewell for Keane while sports analysts treat his 2042 playing future as an open statistical question [15, 22, 23, 25].
* **Entering Cycle 113:** The city awaits official confirmation on whether Vinnie Keane will play in 2042 or retire, and how Mike Paulson resolves offseason contract math for Aitken, Keane, and Dillon [14, 15, 31, 32].

---

### **3. Municipal Emergency Response, Data Discrepancies & Baylight Remediation**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Yu Zen's Injury & EMS Response:** In Cycle 112 (Y3C8), 29-year-old Rockridge resident **Yu Zen** suffered a severe hand injury requiring months of rehabilitation, with EMS Director **Priya Narang** holding his open file on her desk and asking if response crews arrived fast enough [33, 34]. Simultaneously, **Celeste Tran's** wire report recorded Yu Zen on morning walks enjoying neighborhood music and new arrivals [33, 35].
* **Response Wait Times & District Data Gaps:**
  * OARI Program Director **Vanessa Tran-Muñoz** (Rockridge) noted a Chinatown emergency call wait was excessively long (stating West Oakland crews would have responded faster) and demanded district-level data transparency [36, 37].
  * District Attorney **Clarissa Dane** (West Oakland) reported an internal data discrepancy for Fruitvale, where internal sheets read **18%** while public files read **23%** [36, 38].
* **Baylight Soil Remediation Calendar:** Baylight Redevelopment Authority Director **Keisha Ramos** (Lake Merritt) confirmed awaiting soil test results for the **C115 review**, which dictates the overall environmental remediation calendar [15, 39].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 113**
* **Dashboard Metrics vs. Lived Emergency:** Corliss, Narang, and Tran-Muñoz infer that municipal spreadsheets obscure life-altering delays on the pavement [33, 34, 36, 37].
* **Entering Cycle 113:** The newsroom is watching whether Priya Narang's EMS speed inquiry receives an official answer, whether DA Dane resolves the 18% vs. 23% Fruitvale data gap, and whether soil test results arrive ahead of the C115 Baylight review [15, 34, 36, 38, 39].

---

### **4. Fruitvale Corridor Pressures, Transit Shifts & Civic Ownership**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Fruitvale Corridor Audit (Jax Caldera):** In Cycle 111 (Y3C7), investigative reporter **Jax Caldera** (`JAX-TIPS`) reported Fruitvale taquerias slammed with lunch lines while official city maps logged sliding sentiment (0.52), falling retail vitality (down 2.04 to 10.55), and rising **Housing Pressure (+1.00 to 4.5, ranking 17th of 22)** [4, 40-42].
* **Unassigned Program Footprints:** Two active city programs (**Oakland Alternative Response Initiative** and **Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline**) list Fruitvale in their footprint on paper, but neither program owns or mitigates housing pressure or retail decay [4, 43]. Transit hub Phase II plans remain curled in storefront windows, sitting unadvanced at **Visioning** [4, 44].
* **12th Street & Systemwide Transit Shifts:**
  * In Cycle 111 (Y3C7), **12th St Oakland City Center Station** lost **15,192 riders** (down to 8,293 boardings, 86% on-time) as total 8-station ridership dropped to 36,303 boardings [45-48].
  * AC Transit operators **Evan Lewis**, **Calvin Mwangi**, **Ray Neal**, and mechanic **Joel Wren** cited pedestrian blockages, dust, and detours from ongoing **Baylight District construction** as the primary cause of platform desertion [45, 47, 49-51].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 113**
* **The Ownership Void:** Jax Caldera and Mags Corliss infer that placing a neighborhood inside a program's footprint on paper serves as administrative window dressing while no city official assumes direct ownership of rising rent pressure [4, 42, 43, 52, 53].
* **Entering Cycle 113:** The newsroom is watching whether any municipal leader takes ownership of Fruitvale's housing slide and whether upcoming City Council votes on Baylight construction force transit platforms to fill back in [14, 49, 52, 54].

---

### **5. East Oakland Community Programs & Institutional Hand-offs**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Foothill Baptist Tabernacle Baseline:** **Foothill Baptist Tabernacle** in East Oakland operates a food pantry (mutual-aid) and a seniors lunch program (health), both active on the public record since **Cycle 78** [55-57].
* **Demographic Census (Cycle 112):** East Oakland counts **327 seniors** (up 1), **476 students** (up 2), and **1,535 adults** (up 5) [56, 58]. The hospital census logged 123 sick residents, 2 admissions, and 4 in care (4 beds occupied, un-tracked/unnamed) [58]. Justice census logged 6 charges, 1 arrest, and 2 in custody [58].
* **Program Founders vs. Local Address:**
  * Eight active programs exist in East Oakland in Cycle 112 [55, 57].
  * The **Mark Aitken Youth Baseball League** was founded by A's legend Mark Aitken (who resides in Jack London) [55, 57, 59].
  * The **Eastside Hoopers Coalition** was founded by Marcus Whitfield (who resides in Fruitvale) [55, 57, 60].
  * Neither founder lives on the East Oakland block where his program operates [55, 57].
* **Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline:** Council Member **Janae Rivers** highlighted the launch of the **Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline** in East Oakland as a "first rung of the ladder" while OARI call volumes expand citywide [61].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 113**
* **Institutional Hand-off Gap:** Maria Keen and Mags Corliss infer that programs handed down by non-resident founders lack documented local parent or volunteer input [55, 57, 58, 62].
* **Entering Cycle 113:** The newsroom is tracking where the hand-off occurs between youth sports leagues, Councilmember Rivers's Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline, and lasting family economic stability [62].

---

### **6. Expansion Oakland Oaks & Community Belonging**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Preseason Record & Media Reassurances:** The expansion **Oakland Oaks** finished preseason winless at **0–5 (0–9 overall including rookie camp)** in Cycle 110 [63, 64]. GM **Elliot Abraham** acknowledged early losses and offered media reassurances [55, 63, 64].
* **Jack London Bar Sentiment:** In Jack London bars, patrons **Melton Neilon** (sourdough baker) and **Rick Walker** (teacher) follow games between work shifts without bandwidth for complex statistical columns [55, 63, 65, 66].
* **Draymond Status:** Questions regarding **Draymond's** potential return to the Oaks remained open through Cycle 112 (Y3C8) [55, 63, 64].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 113**
* **Conversation vs. Belonging:** Talia Finch and Mags Corliss infer that community outreach has brought the team into local conversation, but has not yet earned an unquestioned place in busy residents' lives [55, 63, 64, 67].
* **Entering Cycle 113:** As regular-season play begins, the newsroom is watching whether Jack London patrons glance back at the screens and whether Draymond returns to the roster [14, 55, 64].

---

### **7. Media Audits, Mention Ledgers & Broadcast Standings**

#### **Direct Published Facts**
* **Mention Ledger Metrics (Celeste Tran Wire, Y3C8):**
  * **Jade Orion** (Lake Merritt musician): Mentions rose to 18; she noted neighborhood life feels unchanged while **Cathedral of the Living Word** volunteers clean streets [15, 35, 68, 69].
  * **Tara Ellison** (Rockridge journalist): Mentions rose to 12; noted covering local news, observing waterfront film crews, and redoing work requested by a *Bay Tribune* manager [15, 70].
  * West Oakland drew 18 new arrivals; Jack London added 12; Fruitvale, Adams Point, and Grand Lake added 7 each [35, 69].
* **UNDOCKED Weekly Digest Board (Nia Rook, Y3C8):**
  * **Eric Taveras** holds the #1 spot on the UNDOCKED board for the second straight cycle (streak at 2) [71].
  * **Sammie Alvarez** (Civic Reporter): Credits dropped by 209 after two flights; expressed uncertainty about whether Temescal community energy translates into action [71, 72].
  * **Rafael Phillips** (Nurse Aide): Credits stayed flat at 0 across two flights; noted tight finances [71, 72].
  * **Iris Pham:** Credits gained 1 across one episode [71, 73].

#### **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines for Cycle 113**
* **Ledger Counts vs. Block Reality:** Kai Marston, Celeste Tran, and Mags Corliss infer that mention spikes and media rankings represent parallel statistical metrics rather than direct evidence of street-level community change [15, 52, 69, 74, 75].
* **Entering Cycle 113:** The UNDOCKED digest will show whether Eric Taveras maintains his #1 lead and whether Sammie Alvarez's Temescal reporting translates local energy into civic results [71-73].

references.cited_text: The money is real and it is moving. The West Oakland Stabilization Fund carries a $28,000,000 budget, with $22,600,000 still remaining, and its latest disbursement landed this cycle, Cycle 111: a month-ten payment of $400,000. Avery Santana, who proposed the Fund, announced that approval in two statements. "Month-ten disbursement approved — $400,000 to keep West Oakland families in their homes," she said at the gavel. At the open, she added: "The families who qualified for this money six months ago shouldn't wait another day." Brenda Okoro put the stakes in the same terms: "Stabilization is a race against displacement — month-ten disbursement keeps us ahead."

The Fund's path to this point runs through a single vote. In Cycle 78 the measure passed 6-3, against a required threshold of 6-3, and Santana signed it that cycle. The record names three of the nine seats: Ramon Vega voted yes, Leonard Tran voted no, and Elliott Crane voted yes remotely. The file does not place the other six, and this ledger will not infer them from a tally. Denise Carter, whose District 1 office issued this cycle's council statement, framed the Fund's reach around movement rather than fixed addresses: "When storefronts go quiet, families go next—so we're taking the Stabilization Fund to where the need is moving." That sentence points at a geography the tracker does not map. The Initiative is logged to West Oakland, and nothing in the file breaks the $400,000 down by block, by household, or by case.

Both statements describe the same event, a $400,000 month-eleven disbursement from the West Oakland Stabilization Fund, approved in Cycle 112. The tracker records it as the fund's latest milestone, and it is the first thing this ledger can confirm about the fund this cycle. The fund's paper trail starts in Cycle 78. The Initiative carries a $28 million budget and a 6-3 vote requirement, and it passed that cycle 6-3. The Initiative was proposed by Avery Santana, and the mayor signed it that same cycle. The record names three of the nine council seats on that vote: Ramon Vega voted yes, Leonard Tran voted no, and Elliott Crane voted yes remotely. The supplied record does not place the votes of the other six seats, so this ledger does not reconstruct the tally beyond the 6-3 result.

Jax Caldera found the mirror image in Fruitvale, a lunch line out the door at the taqueria while the neighborhood's own readings slide. Mood is still near the top of the city and retail still sits well above the middle, but both are dropping and housing pressure is climbing. Two programs list Fruitvale in their footprint, and neither owns the problem that's actually hurting it. Jax asked who answers for that, and no one with a title would say. I'd add one thing. Carmen Delaine reported on the West Oakland Stabilization Fund, where Marcus Webb says ninety-one households are stabilized and every file will survive an audit. Another $400,000 went out this week, and the processing standard held at twenty-three days. Carmen was honest that an average hides the slowest case, and the record doesn't show whether any family waited far longer. Councilmember Denise Carter said the Fund is being taken to where the need is moving. Fine. Jax is standing in a place where the need appears to be moving, and the Fund isn't listed there.

============================================================ By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic Ninety-One Households, One Ledger "Ninety-one households stabilized means ninety-one West Oakland families who won't face displacement this month," Marcus Webb said on the record this cycle, "and every case file meets compliance standards that will survive audit." The statement is the only place in this cycle's record where the Stabilization Fund is counted by household rather than by dollar, and it is the figure the city is standing on.

The same gap between the record and the room runs through the money. Carmen Delaine's ledger confirms that month eleven of the West Oakland Stabilization Fund cleared at $400,000, matching month ten, with the 23-day standard held. The mayor's office put out two statements that both praised it. Marcus Webb, who runs the disbursements, wrote a quieter version after work. Six files are still waiting on title search, and the standard doesn't tell him which of those households is one missed payment from losing everything. He walked past a couple of the addresses, saw the lights on, and didn't stop. The spreadsheet says they're ahead. The spreadsheet never has to sit in a kitchen and explain a delay. That is the contradiction I'd put at the top of anyone's list, a program that can be on schedule and still have six kitchens waiting.

============================================================ By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic West Oakland Stabilization Fund: Month Eleven Clears The mayor's office put it in writing this cycle, in two statements. The first came from the gavel: "Month-eleven, 23-day standard maintained — this fund delivers because Brenda Okoro's team treats every application like family." The second, from the opening, was blunter: "West Oakland families don't need promises—they need checks that clear. Month-eleven disbursement approved."

The money has moved in steps. The tracker lists a $22.2 million remaining balance against the $28 million total, and cumulative disbursements above $5 million. Month-ten, approved in Cycle 111, was also $400,000. Month-eleven, approved this cycle, matches it. The processing standard has held at 23 days across both approvals, and the record shows no change to that figure. The clock runs forward. The next scheduled action is a month-twelve disbursement review in Cycle 113. That review is the next point at which the record will show whether the pattern of two identical $400,000 approvals continues. The tracker does not yet say what the month-twelve amount will be, and this ledger will not guess.

What the Packet does establish is this: the Fund moved $400,000 on schedule, the processing standard held, and the city's account of the families involved is one household count and one compliance claim, both from the office that runs the Fund. What it does not establish is where the money lands once it leaves the treasury, which block, which tenant, or which landlord. The city treasury took in $5.1M this cycle and closed at $110.3M, and nothing in the file traces the Fund's dollars through that balance.

The city treasury gives the fund its context without explaining it. This cycle the treasury took in $5.1 million: $5 million from the weekly budget allocation and $122,035 in court money from 27 cleared charges. The balance closed at $115.4 million, up from $110.3 million. The record connects none of those figures to the fund's disbursements, and this ledger does not connect them either. What the record establishes is narrow. The fund is in its disbursement phase. Approvals are on schedule. The processing standard is held. What it does not establish is the far end of the pipe. The supplied record contains no account of how the approved money reached West Oakland households, which applications it covered, or what changed for the people it was meant for. The phrase "treats every application like family" describes an office's conduct. It is not a measure of outcomes, and the record offers no outcome data to set beside it.

============================================================ By Ines Sorensen | Bay Tribune Culture Month eleven’s done, $400K moved, and the queue’s finally down to six files waiting on title search. I keep telling myself twenty-three days is fine, it’s the standard, but the standard doesn’t tell me which of those six households is one missed payment from losing it all. I walked past a couple of the addresses on my way home—didn’t stop, just saw the lights on, and that’s the whole game, isn’t it. The spreadsheet says we’re ahead, but the spreadsheet never has to sit in a kitchen and explain a delay. Tomorrow I’ll push the title vendor again, and tonight I’ll just let the numbers sit.

The clock is the strongest part of the record. Month-nine, in Cycle 110, cleared at $400,000 with a 23-day average processing time. Cycle 111 held the 23-day processing standard again. The next action is the month-eleven disbursement review in Cycle 112. An average is a single number, and the file carries no case-level processing times. A 23-day mean can hold cases that took far longer, and the record does not say whether any did. Two neighboring Initiatives show the same pattern of announced money and thin public accounting. The West Oakland Tenant Defense Fund is scheduled for a vote in Cycle 112 at a $4.2M budget. Commercial Stabilization for Grand Lake sits at legislation-filed with $2.5M. Neither is in disbursement, and neither has a payment on the books this cycle.

That gap sits between two offices. The mayor's statements speak for the approval and the clock. The tracker holds the dollars and the dates. Neither supplies household-level results, and neither is asked in the supplied record to produce them before the month-twelve review. The Initiative's own success measure is the 23-day standard. The mayor has said it was maintained, and the record confirms it. If that standard is the measure of success, the question this cycle leaves open is the one the supplied record cannot answer: if the 23-day standard is the measure of success, what is the measure of impact?

Next week I'm watching the month-eleven review for the Stabilization Fund, and whether the case-level times ever come out. I'm watching the council vote on Baylight and whether the platform fills back in. I'm watching Paulson's roster math, and Aitken's name in particular. I'm watching whether anyone claims Fruitvale. And I'm watching the Oaks as their season opens, to see whether anyone in that bar glances back at the screen. ============================================================ THE WEEK'S REPORTING

A few smaller notes. Jade Orion's mentions ticked up to eighteen and she says nothing around Lake Merritt feels different, which is the most grounded thing anyone said about fame all week. Tara Ellison mentioned being asked to redo work, and I'll just say that's part of the job here and she did it. And Keisha Ramos is waiting on soil test results for the C115 review, which will tell us something about what Baylight can promise. Next week I'm watching four things. The month-twelve disbursement review comes up in Cycle 113, and I want to see whether the six waiting files shrink or just get quieter. I'm watching for any word on what Keane is actually doing, playing or leaving, because the city deserves a straight answer before the next toast. I'm watching Yu Zen's hand, and whether the system that got to him can answer Narang's question. And I'm watching that eighteen and twenty-three in Fruitvale until someone tells us which is true.

Then there's the part of the week that was just joy, with a cost attached. The A's won the title, and Anthony Raines laid out Game Five. John Ellis threw six innings with two earned runs and five strikeouts. Eric Taveras homered and drove in two. Darrin Davis had three hits and a homer, and Mark Aitken added one more. Anthony also reminded us that one night is one night. It was the seventh championship under Mike Paulson, and Paulson and Taveras both show up in Nia Rook's undocked reporting as well. I won't guess at what's in it beyond that. But it matters that the man on the parade bus and the man at the plate are also in a file about something else. A championship doesn't suspend the rest of a person's life. It sits on top of it.

On the feed, those three numbers are the whole of his box for the night, and they are enough to explain why the A's are one win from the cup of their chapter and why the rest of the lineup's stat lines read as support rather than headline. The club's team record on the feed stands at 4-1 with a three-game winning streak, and Game Five completed the sequence that delivered the A's their seventh World Series title under Mike Paulson.

The hitters carried the rest of the sheet. Eric Taveras went 1HR and 2RBI, which is the power the club needed in a game that was not going to be decided by singles. Darrin Davis put up 1HR, 2RBI and a 3-4 night, the most complete offensive line the feed records for any Game Five bat. Mark Aitken added 1HR and 1RBI. The feed frames Taveras as the source of the power and the two veterans, Davis and Aitken, as the contributors around him, and the stat lines support that division: three players with home runs, two of them with multiple runs driven in, one a three-hit night from the middle of the order.

Tanya Cruz took us onto that bus. Paulson, Vinnie Keane and Benji Dillon rode at the front, waving, and back in the clubhouse the confetti was still in their sleeves. Aitken said the quiet moments are where the weight sits, and that nobody knows what's next. Benji talked about the quiet after the noise, when you realize you don't have to do it again. Paulson said the part nobody sees is doing the math on who stays and who goes while the confetti is still in your hair. For Paulson, the manager, that math is the job, and it starts the day after the parade. The city got a party, and he got a roster problem. Both are true, and the city should remember the second one while it's celebrating the first.

Across the eight stations, ridership totaled 36,303 in Cycle 111, compared with 91,564 in the prior cycle. That is a large change in the system’s use, but the record also marks the cycle as a holiday period with events in Downtown, Fruitvale, Dimond, East Oakland, Jack London, Rockridge and Piedmont Ave. Those conditions complicate any clean explanation. “I’ve been noticing fewer folks at the 12th Street station lately, even though the buses are running smoother than ever,” Wren said. “It’s strange—people used to pack in there, but now it feels quieter. Maybe it’s the Baylight construction approvals making folks rethink their routes. Hard to say, but something’s shifted.” The fare gate continues its small mechanical argument with each person who uses it. The schedule can be better while the station becomes less useful. On-time performance measures whether service arrives when expected. Ridership measures whether people still choose to be there. A system can improve the first measure and lose the second.

Calvin Mwangi, an AC Transit bus driver, said he has not heard regular riders identify 12th Street as a specific avoidance point. “Nah, can't say I've heard my regulars talk much about avoiding 12th Street specifically,” Mwangi said. “Most folks just grumble about the usual—delays, construction, you know how it is. It does establish that Baylight District construction is active around Downtown, while the station posted its largest decline among the eight stations tracked this cycle. “You know, it's funny—on paper, the numbers look good, right? Better on-time stats should mean happier riders. But driving the route, I see it different. ============================================================ By Kai Marston | Bay Tribune Culture Tara Ellison Is Rising, and Nobody Around Her Can Say Where Tara Ellison is standing on a Rockridge sidewalk with her hands loose at her sides, and when the question comes she takes a second before she answers. "I'm not sure what you mean. I'm just here in Rockridge, and I'm not in a room with anyone right now." The ledger has a different account of her. This cycle it lists Ellison as a journalist in Media, Rockridge, climbing fast enough that it flags her as surging. Her name sits among the 39 culture figures the ledger counts as rising this cycle, and one of those 39 is new to the record. She was last logged the cycle before this one. Between those two points, the ledger doesn't say what she did, only that the numbers moved her up.

The ledger keeps its own balance. It has moved Lena Cross and Rowan Pierce onto its where-are-they-now file, a quieter list for names that have stopped climbing. Rising and fading sit in the same record, and the same neighborhoods hold both. Walking back toward the car, I kept thinking about how little of this is visible. Ellison's rise is real on the ledger. Vasquez's bassline is real at a light in Laurel. Reyes's indifference is real in Fruitvale. None of those three places touches the others in any way I can document. A surge in one name does not prove a neighborhood is moving, and a neighborhood humming with music does not prove that a single name is the reason.
